I have the same issue and tried debug a little bit. This following paragraph is the analysis from Opus 4.7. Could be worthwhile putting into a context for fixing this crashing issue.

Opus 4.7 analysis
-------

Adding another v1.15.1 data point with a different escalation path: same root-cause signature, but in our case it terminates the whole TUI process via Bun SIGTRAP rather than just logging the rejection.
## Environment
- opencode `1.15.1` (also reproduced on `1.15.3`)
- bundled `Bun v1.3.13 (bf2e2cec)`
- macOS 26.3.1 (Apple M2)
- terminal: Ghostty / xterm-ghostty
- Reproduced on two separate M2 machines, both running curl-installed opencode
`v1.15.0` does not exhibit this — confirmed by downgrade (`opencode upgrade 1.15.0`) on both machines.
## Trigger
TUI session with an active subagent (`Sisyphus - Ultraworker` parent → `@explore` subagent). Pressing **Ctrl+X** to switch into the running subagent session reliably triggers the chain. On the second occurrence, the parent TUI crashes to terminal with a Bun panic.
## Log signature (sanitized, from `~/.local/share/opencode/log/`)
```text
INFO  service=session  id=ses_<parent>  version=1.15.1  agent=Sisyphus - Ultraworker  created
INFO  service=session  id=ses_<child>   version=1.15.1  parentID=ses_<parent>  title=Map auth module surface (@explore subagent)  created
...
INFO  service=lsp.client  serverID=elixir-ls  path=/.../lib/.../router.ex     workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles
INFO  service=lsp.client  serverID=elixir-ls  path=/.../lib/.../scope.ex      workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles
ERROR service=default     e=InstanceRef not provided rejection
INFO  service=session.prompt  session.id=ses_<child>   cancel
INFO  service=session.prompt  session.id=ses_<parent>  cancel
INFO  service=lsp.client  serverID=elixir-ls  path=/.../lib/.../user_auth.ex  workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles
ERROR service=session.processor  session.id=ses_<parent>  error=Aborted process
ERROR service=session.processor  session.id=ses_<parent>  error=Aborted process
```
So this matches the exact path you identified: `LSP client` initialised → `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` → `InstanceRef not provided` from inside `Bus.publish` in `lsp.ts`. Same call site, `elixir-ls` instead of `remark`.
## Escalation: process-level SIGTRAP
On the next user input after this rejection, the whole TUI crashes with a Bun panic instead of a clean rejection:
```text
Bun v1.3.13 (bf2e2cec) macOS Silicon
macOS v26.3.1
panic: Segmentation fault at address 0x13D30
SIGTRAP
```
Stack (from `bun.report`):
```
parcel-watcher.node
napi_call_threadsafe_function
ThreadSafeFunction.scheduleDispatch
ConcurrentTask.createFrom
```
Bun report: https://bun.report/1.3.13/Ma1bf2e2cemxHuhoqC_2+iydmmqhZ_____A2Agz+E
My read on the escalation:
- `lsp.ts:294` rejection aborts the session processor mid-flight while `@parcel/watcher` still holds an NAPI threadsafe function reference back into the Effect runtime.
- The next callback from the native watcher thread fires `napi_call_threadsafe_function` into a callback whose surrounding Effect scope has been torn down, dereferencing freed memory inside Bun's `ConcurrentTask.createFrom`.
- This is consistent with the NAPI deferred-finalizer bug class Bun fixed in `1.3.14` ([release notes](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.3.14)). opencode bundles `1.3.13`, so the underlying NAPI race is latent — `v1.15.0` happens to avoid tripping it; the v1.15.1 `InstanceRef` rejection path appears to trip it on subagent transition.
The `parcel-watcher` callback site in `packages/opencode/src/file/watcher.ts` also changed in v1.15.1 (`InstanceState.bind` → `EffectBridge.make().bind`), which is the other call site I'd suspect of dangling-callback-after-scope-end. Worth checking whether the bridge finalizer can run while parcel's native thread still has the callback pointer in flight.

Our provider emits OpenAI Responses-style structural completion events, but not enough SDK-friendly finish classification for opencode’s current parser. OpenAI Responses itself does not require finish_reason; the client must derive a finish classification from the event stream. The change in this PR works because it treats the unmapped completed function-call step as "other" instead of leaving it undefined.

Operator note from an adjacent project — we've been running RLM (via [`alexzhang13/rlm`](https://github.com/alexzhang13/rlm), the paper's own reference implementation) as a memory-system orchestrator in production for ~3 weeks, on a 274K-drawer palace + 200-question Cat-9a-shaped retrieval eval. Adds three operational caveats to the "RLM is production-ready" framing that aren't in the published numbers:

**1. Base model choice matters more than RLM-the-framework.** Same RLM wrapper, same task, same retrieval substrate — `gemma4:e4b` lands at 0.417 mean recall; `qwen3.5:4b` lands at 0.717 (+30pp at fixed 4B params). The published Tau2 tool-use benchmark predicts this almost exactly — qwen3.5 leads gemma4 by 37.7 Tau2 points. So when OpenCode adds RLM, the **base model's tool-use training is the dominant variable**, not the RLM scaffold. The published "91% BrowseComp+ with RLM" numbers presumably use a capable base; with a 4B local model the floor is much lower.

**2. The RLM "model writes code to query what it needs" assumes the model *will* write the code.** On our 30-question diagnostic, gemma4 chose to answer from prior knowledge on **18/30 questions (60% zero-call rate)** — never invoked the search tool at all. qwen3.5 zero-called on only 4/30 (13%). RLM's elegance depends on the model deciding to invoke; lower-discipline models defeat the paradigm. Two-axis sub-test:

| | Invocation rate (P(tool_calls ≥ 1)) | Recall conditional on invocation |
|---|---|---|
| gemma4:e4b | 40% | 0.625 |
| qwen3.5:4b | 87% | 0.750 |

The 30pp recall gap decomposes ~50/50 into "does the model invoke?" and "what does it do with the result?"

**3. Prompt-engineering controls partially close the gap.** We prepended a `MANDATORY RETRIEVAL CONSTRAINT` directive to RLM's standard system prompt (system-prompt-only, no library change). gemma4 lifted from 0.417 → **0.567 at n=5 (+15pp)** and → **0.724 at n=20 (+30.7pp)** on the same task. The fix touches one constructor kwarg ([example](https://github.com/techempower-org/multipass-structural-memory-eval/blob/feat/rlm-adapter/sme/adapters/rlm_adapter.py)) and surfaces as `invocation_mode="forced"` in our wrapper. Caveat: at n=20 the same intervention *regressed* qwen3.5 (0.883 at n=5 → 0.850 at n=20) — forced retrieval interacts non-additively with retrieval breadth. Recommendation for the OpenCode side: expose a system-prompt-augmentation knob alongside the RLM tool surface, not just the tool surface; and sweep `k` rather than fixing it. Low-discipline base models become usable when invocation isn't optional; high-discipline models can be hurt by over-forcing.

**4. The substrate can already beat the orchestrator.** Raw `mempalace-daemon` (no LLM orchestration, just hybrid postgres+pgvector+AGE retrieval) hits **0.733 recall** on the same corpus where gemma4-RLM lands at 0.417. The orchestrator was *actively dropping* signal the substrate provided for free. RLM's value isn't automatic — it requires the base model to use retrieved content well. Worth measuring "RLM lift vs raw retrieval" as a separate axis in OpenCode's benchmarks; we expect non-trivial regressions on small models.

---

Full per-model breakdown and the forced-invocation comparison live on the [SME tracking issue](https://github.com/M0nkeyFl0wer/multipass-structural-memory-eval/issues/3#issuecomment-4468157343) (`M0nkeyFl0wer/multipass-structural-memory-eval#3`) — Step 2-forced (4 conditions × n=5/n=20) just landed with the full table and decomposition. Cross-linking here in case the empirical lens helps shape OpenCode's RLM rollout.

The published RLM numbers are real, but they're a ceiling that depends on (a) base-model tool-use quality and (b) the model choosing to invoke. Both are configurable; both deserve first-class surfaces in any RLM integration. 🫏

Also worth noting: this PR prevents cross-project context pollution. Each WebSocket server writes its own lock file with the correct `workspaceFolders` for that VS Code window. The TUI's `resolveEditorLockFile` already scores lock files by workspace path match — so opencode running in project A won't pick up selections from a VS Code window opened on unrelated project B, unlike the current situation where users with only the Claude Code extension installed can see context bleeding across unrelated sessions.

Related: #26852 (stale `CLAUDE_CODE_SSE_PORT` can also cause cross-session contamination — our extension provides a clean, workspace-scoped lock file alternative).

I experienced this issue between 5/11 - 5/13 using both `anthropic` and `openai-compatible`. On 5/13, I manually patched OpenCode `1.14.50` to use a KimiCLI User-Agent:

```
perl -i -pe 's/"User-Agent": `opencode\/\$\{InstallationVersion\}`/"User-Agent": (process.env.OPENCODE_USER_AGENT || "KimiCLI\/1.37.0")/g' opencode/packages/opencode/src/session/llm.ts
```

That fixed the issue and I have not received the error since. Others on the [Kimi Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1369594130807787570/1504145688278204446) continue to report the error. Those that apply the patch also report that replacing the User-Agent resolves the issue.

To the OCA users of opencode:
I found an OCA upstream Responses streaming issue while debugging OpenCode visibility failures. For some /v1/responses stream=true post-tool requests, upstream returns HTTP 200 but then closes the SSE stream with no useful output, sometimes only lifecycle events or even bytes:0. This happens intermittently across endpoints, so it does not look like a single bad endpoint or issue with opencode. The workaround in this PR was forcing opencode to do a retry. I added OCA proxy-side protection to hide those broken attempts from the client and retry before committing downstream SSE, which resolved the OpenCode rendering issue in my local testing. We need to bring this issue to OCA team now.

@kitlangton This PR introduces a regression.

Parent agents with scoped edit permissions like:

```yaml
edit:
  "*": deny
  "specific-pattern": allow
```

now break subagents that have their own scoped edit allows:

```yaml
edit:
  "other-pattern": allow
```

`other-pattern` can no longer be accessed.

Merging of permissions puts parent's `"*": deny`  last, overwriting any allow rules by child.

The root cause was likely in opentui's ScrollBox. `recalculateBarProps` (triggered by content size changes during streaming) reset `_hasManualScroll` to false when the user had scrolled up, causing the viewport to jump. This was fixed upstream in opentui PR #722 (merged Feb 21, in 0.2.11+). I dug into this locally and have a patch that improves this a lot, but does not fully eliminate the very last 1-2 flashes when the message settles.

What I found
- The regression seems to line up with the switch back to the TUI markdown renderable in `v1.14.50` (`flip back to markdown renderable`).
- In `packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/routes/session/index.tsx`, assistant text currently streams through `<markdown streaming={true} internalBlockMode="top-level" ... />`.
- While a trailing fenced code block is growing, the top-level markdown structure keeps getting rebuilt/re-highlighted, which is what causes the visible flicker.
- Plain text is much smoother because the block structure stays stable.

What I tried locally
1. Split `settled head + trailing open fenced tail`
   - render the settled head as non-streaming markdown
   - render the growing tail as a separate code renderable
   - result: removes most of the flicker during streaming, but there are still 1-2 final flashes when the message settles

2. Keep the trailing fenced block isolated even after the closing fence arrives
   - result: removes the bigger whole-block flash near the end
   - but depending on how the code renderable mode is switched, this can reintroduce token-level syntax flicker on identifiers like `main` / `print`

3. Force the isolated tail code renderable to `streaming={false}` immediately
   - result: much worse; redraws become more aggressive

4. Keep the isolated trailing code block in `streaming={true}` until the assistant message completes
   - result: similar overall to (1) on my machine; much better than baseline, but it still leaves 1-2 final flashes right when the assistant message settles

Files touched in the local experiment
- `packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/routes/session/index.tsx`
- `packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/routes/session/streaming-markdown.ts`
- `packages/opencode/test/cli/tui/streaming-markdown.test.ts`

Validation
- added focused tests for the fenced-code splitter
- `bun test test/cli/tui/streaming-markdown.test.ts` passes
- `bun run typecheck` passes

Current take
- There is definitely a useful app-side mitigation here.
- But the remaining final flash looks like it may be at/near the OpenTUI markdown/code streaming settle path, rather than just opencode's wrapper logic.

If helpful, I can clean up the current patch into a PR, but I wanted to post the investigation/results first because the last bit probably needs maintainer/upstream input.

I’d make this a terminal state rather than another retry path. A useful regression test would force overflow, make compaction return the same-or-larger token count (or an error), then verify the runner:

1. attempts compaction at most N times,
2. records before/after token counts and the compaction reason,
3. stops further model calls with a state like `compaction_failed` / `blocked_context_overflow`,
4. preserves the last successful turn plus a recovery handoff, and
5. tells the user the exact next recovery action: export/clear/restart or remove the uncompressible payload.

Without the before/after token receipt, an infinite compact loop can look like progress while only spending credits.
